summary: An early Telnet option, from 1974, for agreeing how a formfeed character in output is handled. A formfeed traditionally tells a printer or terminal to start a new page or clear the screen. The option lets the two ends settle that between them. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines the Telnet NAOFFD option for agreeing how output formfeeds are handled. The sender and receiver can negotiate which party handles them and what action to take.

subtitle: A Telnet option for negotiating which side handles output formfeeds.

tldr.problem: A Telnet sender and receiver may need to agree on which party handles formfeed characters in output.
tldr.mechanism: The NAOFFD option uses Telnet negotiation and subnegotiation values to specify a formfeed handler and disposition.
tldr.outcome: RFC 655 is Historic. It says the receiver handles formfeeds if neither party chooses to do so, and the sender handles them if both choose to.

today: RFC 655 has Historic status. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The NAOFFD Option
sections.content:
NAOFFD means Negotiate About Output Formfeed Disposition. The option code is 13. It applies to a simplex connection, as described in the Telnet NAOL and NAOP option specifications.

DO and WILL request or agree to negotiate, while DON'T and WON'T refuse negotiation or return to the unnegotiated default. If negotiation is agreed and there is no further subnegotiation, the receiver is assumed to handle output formfeeds.
sections.plainLanguage: NAOFFD lets the sender and receiver negotiate how to handle output formfeeds. Without further subnegotiation, the receiver is assumed to handle them after agreement.

sections.title: Subnegotiation Values
sections.content:
After option negotiation, the sender can use the DS subcommand with an 8-bit value, and the receiver can use DR with an 8-bit value. DS has code 1 and DR has code 0. Either side specifies which party should handle formfeeds and what disposition is suggested.

Value 0 suggests that the command sender alone handle formfeeds. Values 1 to 250 suggest that the other party handle them, with a suggested number of character-times to wait or NUL characters to insert. Value 251 suggests replacing each occurrence with carriage-return/line-feed; 252 suggests discarding it; 253 suggests simulating it; 254 suggests waiting for a character on the other simplex connection; and 255 makes no suggestion about how the other party handles it.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver exchange an 8-bit value to suggest who handles the formfeed and what action to take. The values describe delays, replacement, discarding, simulation, waiting or no specific suggestion.

sections.title: Default and Selection Rules
sections.content:
By default, neither party is required or prohibited from handling formfeeds, though the RFC says it is appropriate for at least the receiver to handle them in a basic way.

If neither side wants to handle formfeeds, the receiver must do so. If both sides want to handle them, the sender gets to handle them, taking any suggestions from the receiver into account. The RFC also says negotiation changes should be acknowledged and a refused option should not be proposed again until something changes.
sections.plainLanguage: If neither party wants to handle formfeeds, the receiver does. If both want to handle them, the sender does, while considering the receiver's suggestions.
